findings.title: Blocked-email lookup can be bypassed by changing email case
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact where(email: email) lookup using the raw user-supplied value, and neither BlockedEmail nor EmailValidator downcases or strips the address before storage or lookup; User.new_from_params also assigns the submitted email unchanged. PostgreSQL string comparison and the unique index are case-sensitive, so an address blocked as bad@spam.example can register as Bad@SPAM.example, and BlockedEmail rows differing only by case can coexist. Normalize the email (for example with Email.downcase and strip) both when creating BlockedEmail records and when checking them.

findings.title: Validation has a write side effect and counts one signup attempt multiple times
findings.body: EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves the BlockedEmail row. Validation is not a single commit-time event: UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so one blocked signup attempt increments the counter twice. Any other valid? check, or a save that ultimately fails for an unrelated reason such as the password, also records a match even though no account attempt completed. Separate the pure blocked check from hit recording, or record the hit only once at the point an attempt is actually rejected.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: should_block? loads the BlockedEmail row, does record.match_count += 1 in memory, and saves it. Two concurrent attempts with the same blocked email can both read the same count and both write count+1, losing one hit; the full-row save can also overwrite concurrent changes to the record. Use an atomic database increment such as update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...") or increment_counter instead.

findings.title: rejectedEmails is shared mutable state on the controller prototype
findings.body: rejectedEmails is initialized as Em.A([]) in the class definition passed to extend(). In Ember, mutable array/object values declared this way live on the prototype and are shared rather than copied per instance, and createAccount mutates that array with pushObject while nothing ever clears it. Rejected addresses can therefore leak across controller instances and remain rejected for the lifetime of the app/session instead of being scoped to one account-creation flow. Initialize the array per instance (for example in init) and reset it when the create-account modal is shown or closed.
